sections.title: How does the AP® lang score calculator work?
sections.html:
The AP® lang score calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports composite score (0-100) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the reading (0-45), the question 1 – Synthesis (0-6), the question 2 – Rhetorical (0-6) and the question 3 – Argument (0-6).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

sections.title: The formula behind the AP® lang score calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Composite score (0-100)=rounded, ((55 ÷ 18) × question 3 – Argument (0-6) + (55 ÷ 18) × question 2 – Rhetorical (0-6) + (55 ÷ 18) × question 1 – Synthesis (0-6) + reading (0-45))
AP® score (1-5)=(((rounded, ((55 ÷ 18) × question 3 – Argument (0-6) + (55 ÷ 18) × question 2 – Rhetorical (0-6) + (55 ÷ 18) × question 1 – Synthesis (0-6) + reading (0-45)) >= 75) ? ( 5 ) : ( (((rounded, ((55 ÷ 18) × question 3 – Argument (0-6) + (55 ÷ 18) × question 2 – Rhetorical (0-6) + (55 ÷ 18) × question 1 – Synthesis (0-6) + reading (0-45)) >= 65) ? ( 4 ) : ( (((rounded, ((55 ÷ 18) × question 3 – Argument (0-6) + (55 ÷ 18) × question 2 – Rhetorical (0-6) + (55 ÷ 18) × question 1 – Synthesis (0-6) + reading (0-45)) >= 53) ? ( 3 ) : ( (((rounded, ((55 ÷ 18) × question 3 – Argument (0-6) + (55 ÷ 18) × question 2 – Rhetorical (0-6) + (55 ÷ 18) × question 1 – Synthesis (0-6) + reading (0-45)) >= 36) ? ( 2 ) : ( 1 ))) ))) ))) )))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Reading (0-45) = 10, Question 1 – Synthesis (0-6) = 10, Question 2 – Rhetorical (0-6) = 10 and Question 3 – Argument (0-6) = 10. The calculator returns Composite score (0-100) = 102 and AP® score (1-5) = 5.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Composite score (0-100) = 102 and AP® score (1-5) = 5 should be roughly the size you expected from Reading (0-45) = 10 and Question 1 – Synthesis (0-6) = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The AP® lang score calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the reading, the question 1 – Synthesis and the question 2 – Rhetorical — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

faq.q: What does the AP® lang score calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns composite score (0-100), derived from the reading, the question 1 – Synthesis and the question 2 – Rhetorical. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the AP® lang score calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the reading, the question 1 – Synthesis, the question 2 – Rhetorical and the question 3 – Argument, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Composite score (0-100) = 102. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the AP® lang score calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
